[PATH:empirical] Matched employer-employee panel data (e.g., LEHD or administrative data) linked to firm-level R&D expenditure records for US firms (2000-2020) — Directly tests wage effects of high-skilled immigration by comparing wage trajectories of native skilled workers within firms that vary in their R&D investment, isolating the conditional effect predicted by the hypothesis.

[PATH:empirical] Survey or case-study evidence from tech firms in high-skill immigration hubs (e.g., Silicon Valley, Seattle) on R&D investment decisions and wage-setting practices — Provides qualitative and quantitative data on whether firms that do not invest in complementary R&D indeed experience downward wage pressure on native skilled workers, helping to confirm the firm-level mechanism.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical models of heterogeneous firms and labor demand (e.g., extensions of the Roy model or search-and-matching models with endogenous R&D) — Develops and tests the microfoundations for why R&D complementarity moderates wage effects, offering predictions that can be empirically validated and clarifying boundary conditions.

scope.domain: high-skill labor markets and firm-level innovation

C006.subject: Immigration of high-skilled workers
C006.predicate: increases innovation and economic growth that benefits
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Immigration of high-skilled workers native workers with similar skills]

[PATH:empirical] Borjas, G. J. (2003). 'The Labor Demand Curve Is Downward Sloping: Reexamining the Impact of Immigration on the Labor Market.' Quarterly Journal of Economics. — Provides a canonical empirical framework for estimating the wage and employment effects of immigration on native workers with similar skills, which can be directly applied to high-skilled workers in OECD countries post-2000.

[PATH:empirical] Kerr, W. R., & Lincoln, W. F. (2010). 'The Supply Side of Innovation: H-1B Visa Reforms and U.S. Ethnic Invention.' Journal of Labor Economics. — Examines how high-skilled immigration (via H-1B visas) affects innovation and native employment in tech sectors, offering evidence on complementarity versus substitution effects relevant to the hypothesis.

[PATH:empirical] Peri, G. (2012). 'The Effect of Immigration on Productivity: Evidence from U.S. States.' Review of Economics and Statistics. — Investigates how immigration of high-skilled workers boosts total factor productivity and native wages, providing a direct test of the innovation and economic growth channel for native workers with similar skills.

C007.subject: Immigration of low-skilled workers
C007.object: substitutable native labor in the same skill tier
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Immigration of low-skilled workers substitutable native labor in the same skill tier]

[PATH:empirical] Card (1990) 'The Impact of the Mariel Boatlift on the Miami Labor Market' - natural experiment study — This seminal paper uses the exogenous shock of the Mariel boatlift to test whether a sudden influx of low-skilled immigrants reduces wages of substitutable native workers. Results show minimal wage effects, challenging the hypothesis. Replicating with post-1980 U.S. data and focusing on low-skill markets with strong complementarities could confirm or refute the hypothesis under the specified scope.

[PATH:empirical] Borjas (2003) 'The Labor Demand Curve Is Downward Sloping' - spatial correlations approach — Borjas finds that immigration reduces wages for competing native workers, especially those without a high school diploma, using a skill-cell approach. Applying his methodology to the post-1980 U.S. and isolating low-skill labor markets with strong complementarities would provide direct evidence for or against the hypothesis, addressing the disputed status.

[PATH:theoretical] Ottaviano & Peri (2012) 'Rethinking the Effect of Immigration on Wages' - general equilibrium model with capital adjustment — This paper models how capital complementarities can offset negative wage effects of low-skilled immigration. Extending their model to the specific domain of 'low-skill labor markets with strong complementarities' would clarify whether the hypothesized wage reduction holds under dynamic capital responses, providing theoretical confirmation or refutation.

scope.domain: low-skill labor markets with strong complementarities

C008.subject: Immigration of low-skilled workers
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Immigration of low-skilled workers complementary native labor]

[PATH:empirical] Quarterly Journal of Economics - 'The Impact of Low-Skilled Immigration on Native Employment and Wages' (e.g., Card, 2001; Borjas, 2003) — Classic studies using U.S. Census and CPS data provide estimates of labor demand elasticities and substitution/complementarity effects, directly testing whether low-skilled immigration reduces demand for native workers with complementary skills.

[PATH:theoretical] NBER Working Paper series on task-based models of immigration (e.g., Peri & Sparber, 2009) — Task-based frameworks model complementarity between immigrant and native labor in low-skill markets, allowing simulation of demand shifts under different skill distributions and production technologies, which can confirm or refute the hypothesis.

[PATH:empirical] American Economic Review - 'Immigration and the Demand for Complementary Labor: Evidence from the Construction Sector' (e.g., Orrenius & Zavodny, 2007) — Industry-specific panel data on low-skill sectors with strong complementarities (e.g., construction, agriculture) can isolate the effect of immigrant inflows on native employment and wages, controlling for local labor market conditions.

scope.domain: low-skill labor markets with strong complementarities

C011.subject: Immigration overall
C011.object: average native wages in regions with low labor mobility and rigid housing supply in the long run
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Immigration overall average native wages in regions with low labor mobility and rigid housing supply in the long run]

[PATH:empirical] Quasi-experimental studies on local labor market shocks (e.g., Mariel Boatlift, refugee resettlement) that estimate wage impacts by region, focusing on heterogeneity by housing supply elasticity and labor mobility. — Directly tests the hypothesis by comparing native wage changes in high vs. low housing-supply-elasticity and high vs. low labor mobility regions, using natural experiments to establish causality.

[PATH:theoretical] Spatial equilibrium models incorporating housing supply constraints and frictional labor mobility (e.g., models by Moretti, Glaeser, or Monras). — Provides a formal framework to derive predictions about wage effects under the specified conditions, identifying necessary assumptions and parameter ranges for the hypothesis to hold.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing empirical literature on immigration's wage effects, stratified by local housing supply elasticity and migration cost proxies. — Synthesizes available evidence to assess whether the hypothesized conditional effect is consistently found across studies, thereby confirming or refuting the scope condition.
